phonemes.desc: Voiced velar stop with close front vowel [ɡil] — firm, like the name of a builder.
The second velar with open [a] — the name's hinge.
Final [mɛʃ] — the hushing sibilant š, 'sh' as in 'ship', the sound the ASCII spelling loses.

pronunciation.approximation: 'gil-ga-MESH' — three even, heavy syllables; the final 'sh' is soft, like sand through fingers.

kin.label: Sumerian
kin.form: Bilgames (Bil₃-ga-mes₃), the older form of the name, interpreted as 'the old man became young'

kin.label: Akkadian
kin.form: Gilgameš, the standard form in the epic's own language — the name the epic echoes in its plant of youth

kin.label: Learned tradition
kin.form: written with the divine determinative in later texts — the hero reckoned among the gods and a judge of the dead

pronunciation.note: Gilgameš is Tier 1 by the non-Greek rule: the restoration preserves the caron š, a distinctive letter the ASCII 'Gilgamesh' loses along with its redundant h. The name is Sumerian at root; the Akkadian epic made it the most famous royal name of Mesopotamia.

domains.title: The King Who Sought the Deep
domains.subtitle: Kingship, Friendship, and the Quest Against Death
domains.lead: Gilgameš, king of Uruk, 'two-thirds god and one-third man', is the hero of the oldest great epic we possess. He builds walls, slays the guardian of the Cedar Forest, spurns a goddess, loses his friend, and walks to the end of the world to ask the flood's survivor the only question that matters: must we die?

cards.name: King of Uruk
cards.desc: The epic opens and closes on the walls he built — 'go up on the wall of Uruk and walk around' — kingship as masonry.

cards.name: The Friend
cards.desc: Enkidu, the wild man fashioned from clay to match him; their friendship is the first great love story of literature.

cards.name: The Cedar Journey
cards.desc: The road west to the Cedar Forest and the slaying of Humbaba, its monstrous guardian — fame won at the price of doom.

cards.name: The Flood and the Plant
cards.desc: Utnapishtim's ark, the waters of death, and the plant 'the old man becomes young', stolen by a serpent while the king slept.

symbols.name: The wild bull
symbols.meaning: His own title — the goring wild bull, son of Lugalbanda and the goddess Ninsun.

symbols.name: The walls of Uruk
symbols.meaning: His true immortality, named in the epic's first and last lines.

symbols.name: The cedar
symbols.meaning: The timber of the Cedar Forest, cut for the great door of Uruk.

symbols.name: The plant of youth
symbols.meaning: 'The old man becomes young' — rejuvenation won from the sea's floor and lost to the serpent.

symbols.name: The deluge
symbols.meaning: The flood of Utnapishtim, the deep he alone among men saw and survived to tell.

mythology.lead: The Standard Babylonian epic, 'He who saw the deep', runs from the streets of Uruk to the waters of death. Its twelve tablets hold the first full arc of friendship, loss, and wisdom in world literature — and its last line is a tour of brickwork.

myths.title: Enkidu Comes from the Wild
myths.text: Uruk groans under its young king — Gilgameš harries his people 'like a wild bull on the rampage', claiming the wedding-night privilege no bridegroom can refuse — and the gods answer by fashioning his equal from clay: Enkidu, a wild man who runs with gazelles, eats grass, and wrecks the trapper's snares. The trapper's stratagem became proverbial: send Šamhat the prostitute, and let bread, beer, and seven days of loving make a man of him. It works, and it costs him — Enkidu is diminished and civilized at once, weaker in the wild and kin to everyone. When he hears of Gilgameš's abuses he travels to Uruk and blocks him at the wedding-house door. They wrestle until the doorframe shudders; and the fight ends in embrace. From that day the king has a second self, and the epic has its thesis: civilization is both a loss and a gift, and friendship is the treaty that makes it bearable.

myths.title: The Cedar Forest and Humbaba
myths.text: Hungry for a name that will outlast him, Gilgameš proposes the impossible: the expedition to the Cedar Forest, sacred to Enlil and guarded by the monstrous Humbaba, whose roar is the storm-flood and whose mouth is fire. Enkidu knows that wilderness and begs off — he has walked it — but goes for his friend's sake. The road is paved with dreams: each night the king climbs the mountain-pass to pray, and each dream comes down terrible, and Enkidu, the former wild man, stands at his head and interprets the terror favorable. With the thirteen winds of Šamaš bound around Humbaba, the friends bring him down, pleading and cursing, and fell the great cedar for the door of Uruk. The fame is real — and fatal. The gods have not forgiven the killing of Humbaba and the cutting of the sacred trees, and the two heroes sail home carrying their doom as the timber comes home on the river, sweet-smelling and already marked.

myths.title: The Bull of Heaven and the Decree
myths.text: Back in Uruk the goddess Ištar offers Gilgameš marriage, and he answers with the catalogue of her dead lovers — Dumuzi turned into a bird of grief, the shepherd, the herdsman, the gardener, all used and discarded — and the immortal insult: 'Thou art but a brazier that goes out in the cold, a flimsy door that keeps not the blast' (SB tablet VI). Ištar, shamed, demands the Bull of Heaven from Anu and leads it down to gore the city; its snort opens pits that swallow hundreds of young men. Gilgameš and Enkidu kill it, and Enkidu flings the bull's haunch into the goddess's face. That night Enkidu dreams the judgment: Anu, Enlil, and Ea have conferred, and because Humbaba was slain and the Bull insulted, one of the two must die — and Enlil says: not Gilgameš. The epic's first half ends where its second begins, with the decree that sends the wild man back to clay and the king out of the world after him. The friend made to restrain the king becomes the sacrifice that unmakes him.

myths.title: Across the Waters of Death
myths.text: Clothed in a lion's skin, Gilgameš wanders beyond the maps: to the twin-peaked Mount Mašu, where scorpion-men guard the sun's gate; through the long tunnel of night; down to the garden of jeweled trees whose fruit is lapis and carnelian; to Šiduri the ale-wife behind her veil, who tells him what every wisdom text after her will repeat — eat thy bread, dance and be merry, hold thy child's hand; and at last across the waters of death with the ferryman Ur-šanabi (SB tablets IX–X). There sits Utnapishtim, the mortal whom the gods made deathless after the flood. He tests the king: stay awake six days and seven nights — the one feat that would prove a man worthy of endless life. Gilgameš falls asleep on the first watch, and sleeps seven days. The man who bested Humbaba cannot defeat the smallest of human needs: rest. The flood-hero's wife bakes a loaf for each day he slept, and the loaves, rotting in a row, count out the verdict better than any speech.

myths.title: The Old Man Becomes Young
myths.text: Utnapishtim gives him one last chance: a thorny plant at the bottom of the sea, 'the old man becomes young' — rejuvenation, not immortality, which the gods have put out of mortal reach. Gilgameš ties stones to his feet, dives through the deadly water, and wins the plant, planning to eat it in his own old age. Then, on the road home, at a cool pool, he stops to bathe — and a serpent, drawn by the plant's fragrance, rises from the water, takes it, and sheds its skin as it goes. The king sits down and weeps: not for the serpent, he says bitterly, but for himself — for all the labor spent, and for the endless toil still owed on Uruk's wall. Then he turns for home, brings Ur-šanabi up onto the wall, and shows him the brickwork and the threshold-stone: this, the epic's last line insists, is what a man leaves. The plant was for the body; the wall is for the city; and four thousand years have judged the trade fair.

lore.syncretism: The epic itself was an international text: copies in Akkadian, Hittite, and Hurrian lay in the archives of Hattusa, and scribes from Assur to Ugarit learned it by heart. Its flood story adapts the older Atra-ḫasīs epic and stands, at a further remove, behind the biblical account of Noah — George Smith's reading of the eleventh tablet in 1872 caused a sensation for exactly that reason. Gilgameš lived on in the margins of later religions: a judge of the dead in Mesopotamian incantations and visions of the netherworld, and, astonishingly, a named giant in the Book of Giants known from Qumran and Manichaean fragments, where Humbaba's name survives as Ḥobabish. The Sumerian King List had already made him a god, and the learned tradition kept him 'two-thirds divine' long after Uruk's walls were rubble.
lore.culturalLegacy: Rediscovered in the ruins of Nineveh, Gilgameš became the measure of how old literature is: every generation since 1872 has re-translated him, from scholarly editions to novels and graphic retellings. He anchors the modern study of the flood traditions, of heroic friendship, and of the wisdom genre. Uruk — Warka in Iraq, a UNESCO World Heritage site — still raises its walls where the epic begins and ends. To write Gilgameš with the caron is a small act of philological justice: the š is the sound of the epic's own language, and the ASCII 'sh' is a translator's patch.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The epic of Gilgameš begins with a wall and ends with a wall, and between them lies the whole education of a human being. At first the king believes what strong young kings believe: that the enemy is distance — the Cedar Forest, the far shore, the undying man beyond the sea. Each victory over distance only brings the real enemy closer, until it stands in his own bedchamber: the fact that he will die. The scorpion-men, the ale-wife, the ferryman, and the flood-hero all tell him the same thing in different voices, and he cannot hear it until the serpent takes the plant. Only then, weeping at the water's edge, does he become the hero of wisdom rather than of strength.

What he brings home is not immortality but an account: 'he who saw the deep' — the epic's first line names him by what he saw and reported, not by what he kept. The plant was for the body; the tale is for the city. And so the last gesture of the poem is a tour of masonry: here are the walls, the brickwork, the threshold. Four thousand years have proven the bargain fair. Uruk's walls are dust, but the tale has outlasted every cedar, every serpent, and every king who heard it and was, for a moment, less afraid.

lore.archaeology: The epic's text is archaeology's gift: the fullest copies are the twelve tablets from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (seventh century BCE), excavated in the nineteenth century and held by the British Museum, where George Smith read the flood tablet in 1872. Behind them lie Old Babylonian fragments (the Pennsylvania and Yale tablets), Middle Babylonian copies from Ugarit and Emar, translations from Hattusa in Anatolia, and, oldest of all, the Sumerian Bilgames poems from Nippur and Ur. The historical kernel is modest but real: the Sumerian King List names Gilgameš as fifth king of the First Dynasty of Uruk, and the vast walls of Uruk (Warka, Iraq) still stand where the epic says he built them.
